Mount Pinatubo. Located on the island of Luzon in the Philippines, Mount Pinatubo is an active stratovolcano that erupted cataclysmically in June 1991 after a six-hundred-year period of dormancy. The eruption was the second-largest volcanic eruption of the twentieth century, surpassed only by the 1912 eruption of Novarupta in Alaska. The explosion caused measurable global cooling of approximately zero point five degrees Celsius between 1991 and 1993 by injecting twenty million tons of sulfur dioxide gas into the stratosphere, which formed a global haze of sulfuric acid aerosols. The eruption coincided with Typhoon Yunya, whose torrential rains mixed with the freshly erupted volcanic ash to trigger massive, destructive mudflows called lahars across Central Luzon. The disaster forced the evacuation of Clark Air Base, a major United States military facility located nearby, which was heavily damaged and subsequently abandoned by the military. The slopes of the volcano were home to the indigenous Aeta people, who had resided there for generations and were permanently displaced by the eruption. Mount Pinatubo's global cooling effects connect it to Krakatoa, another Southeast Asian volcano whose eruption had similar global cooling impacts, and to Mount Tambora, an Indonesian volcano whose massive 1815 eruption caused the historic Year Without a Summer.
